title: Risk of peptic ulcer bleeding associated with <scp>H</scp>elicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs, low‐dose aspirin, and antihypertensive drugs: A case‐control study

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Background and Aim</jats:title><jats:p>The associations between antithrombotic or antihypertensive drugs and peptic ulcer bleeding (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PUB</jats:styled-content>) remain unknown, particularly in <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">A</jats:styled-content>sia, where <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>elicobacter pylori</jats:italic> infection is prevalent. This study aims to evaluate the risks of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PUB</jats:styled-content> from antithrombotic drugs, angiotensin <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">II</jats:styled-content> receptor blockers (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ARB</jats:styled-content>s), angiotensin‐converting enzyme (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ACE</jats:styled-content>) inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, α‐blockers, and β‐blockers.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>This prospective hospital‐based case‐control study included 230 patients with endoscopically verified <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PUB</jats:styled-content> and 920 age and sex‐matched controls (1:4) without bleeding on screening endoscopy. Adjusted odds ratios (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>) for the risk of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PUB</jats:styled-content> were determined by conditional logistic regression analysis.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>In multivariate analysis, alcohol consumption (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 2.2; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001), history of peptic ulcer (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 4.8; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001), <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>. pylori</jats:italic> infection (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 2.1; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001), comorbidity index (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 1.1; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.089), nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">NSAID</jats:styled-content>s) (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 2.0; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.025), and low‐dose aspirin (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 2.8; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.003) increased the risk of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PUB</jats:styled-content>, whereas <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>. pylori</jats:italic> eradication (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 0.03; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001), proton pump inhibitors (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PPI</jats:styled-content>s) (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 0.1; <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001), and histamine 2‐receptor antagonists (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>2<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">RA</jats:styled-content>) (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AOR</jats:styled-content>, 0.1;
